title: The O Antiphons
hook: from 17 December churches sing O Wisdom, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Emmanuel

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Lucy and her crown of candles in the Swedish dark. Your line was light in the dark. Whose dim afternoon did you carry a little light into? Day one thousand nine.

O Wisdom. O Root of Jesse. O Key of David. O Emmanuel. Each of these is the opening of a short sung verse, and in the last days before Christmas, churches that pray the evening office sing them one at a time, a new one each night. Monasteries, cathedrals, small parishes with a handful of people in the pews. Every verse begins with that one open syllable, O, and every verse ends by asking for the same thing. If you've ever sung the carol O come, O come, Emmanuel, you've already sung versions of these verses, folded together into one hymn. Today, the O Antiphons.

An antiphon is a short line sung before and after a psalm or canticle, framing it. These ones frame Mary's song, the Magnificat, at evening prayer. What makes them special is that each one calls the coming Christ by a name drawn from the old scriptures, several of them from the prophet Isaiah. Root of Jesse comes from Isaiah. In the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse, the book of Ruth says, was the father of David. The family tree looks cut down to a stump, and a green shoot pushes up anyway. Key of David is from Isaiah too: "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open." A key that opens what is locked. The antiphon asks him to bring out the prisoner who sits in darkness. And Emmanuel comes from Isaiah, taken up by Matthew's Gospel at the birth of Jesus: "and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." So the verses work like a slow walk through the old scriptures, one name a night, each a little picture: wisdom, a shoot from a stump, a key, God with us. And each one ends the same way, with a single word: come. Come and teach us. Come and set us free. Come and save us. That's Advent in one syllable. They belong to Catholic Vespers, and Anglicans and Lutherans who keep the evening office sing them too. Some sing them in Latin, some in English. The familiar hymn took several of them and set them to one tune, so the waiting sounds the same in every verse.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one O and stay with it. Settle, and breathe. Let the names go by slowly. Wisdom. Root of Jesse. Key of David. Emmanuel, God with us. One of them will catch, maybe the key, if something in your life feels locked, or the shoot from the stump, if something feels cut down. Rest there. If you pray, you can say that name with the word that ends every antiphon: O Emmanuel, come. If you don't, hold the picture, and breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Antiphon. A short line sung before and after a psalm, framing it, as these seven do for Mary's song in the last days before Christmas.
Your line: o come, emmanuel. Today, when you hear that carol in a shop or on the radio, remember it's a stack of old prophecies with one word underneath. Day one thousand nine.

howItsDone: In churches that pray evening prayer (Vespers or Evensong), one O antiphon is sung each night in the days before Christmas, before and after the Magnificat; the hymn O come, O come, Emmanuel is sung in Advent in churches of many kinds.

fork.setup: you're writing one of these evening verses for the days before Christmas. you've named Christ "key of David." what do you ask him to do?
options: come and open the locked door, and bring out the prisoner.
come and judge the kings of the earth.
come and build a new temple.
fork.reveal: the antiphon asks the one who opens and none can shut to lead out the prisoner who sits in darkness.

original.note: Hebrew: with us, God — Isaiah 7:14, which Matthew 1:23 renders "God with us."

trapdoor: what you thought: the words of a Christmas carol.
what it means: short evening verses, one a night, calling Christ by names from the old scriptures.
what a scholar hears: root of Jesse, key of David and Emmanuel come from Isaiah, and each antiphon frames the Magnificat at Vespers.

notes: Claims rule: no date (the index hook says 17 December), no count of antiphons, no age or date for the hymn, and the 'ERO CRAS' acrostic is left out.
Isaiah 11:1: KJV ends the verse with a colon ('roots:'); the script ends the quotation with a period. Confirm acceptable.
Antiphon endings ('come and teach us', 'lead out the prisoner who sits in darkness') are paraphrased, not quoted.
'Anglicans and Lutherans who keep the evening office sing them too': confirm the phrasing.
Original: עִמָּנוּ אֵל as written in Isaiah 7:14 (two words); confirm pointing and pronunciation.

Editor: Jesse as David's father now sourced to Ruth 4:17 (added to sources); fork no longer places the 'key of David' verse on the evening before Christmas; 'Catholics sing them' rephrased so it does not imply every Catholic.

Editor 2: not every title comes from the prophets or Isaiah (O Wisdom draws on wisdom literature, O Adonai on Exodus); teach, word and trapdoor now say 'the old scriptures, several from Isaiah' and name only the three Isaiah titles the script cites.
Audit: hook said singers of the hymn had 'already sung these verses'; the hymn paraphrases only some of them, so now 'versions of these verses' (matches the teach's 'took several of them').
